extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, law clerks, and patent-expert witnesses (design- and utility-patent infringement practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate guidance on standards for design- and utility-patent infringement, including claim construction, expert testimony, doctrine of equivalents, and JMOL review. Focuses on how intrinsic and extrinsic evidence govern meaning of claim terms and the permissible role of expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent infringement: ordinary-observer test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove design patent infringement, a patentee must demonstrate that the accused product 'embod[ies] the patented design or any colorable imitation thereof.' Whether a product infringes a design patent hinges on whether an ordinary observer would consider the two designs to be substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ordinary observer is the principal purchaser of the particular product (e.g., a school bus dealer or the purchaser making decisions for a school district). Expert testimony about the ordinary observer's perspective is permitted but not always required. Cases cited: Egyptian Goddess, Top Brand, Gorham, Arminak. Anti-pattern: treating lay or irrelevant viewpoints as the ordinary observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of an expert testifying as to the ordinary observer
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert witness may testify as to the perspective of an ordinary observer even if the expert possesses extraordinary skill, but the expert must establish familiarity with the perspective of that ordinary observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to POSA standards in utility patents: extraordinary skill is not disqualifying but relevance requires showing ordinary-observer familiarity (see FastShip, Ruiz, Kyocera Senco). An expert who cannot show such familiarity may be irrelevant. Courts may permit such testimony if qualifications are timely challenged; failure to timely object can result in forfeiture. Anti-pattern: admitting conclusory expert opinions about the ordinary observer without showing the expert's familiarity with purchaser perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture/timeliness of objections to expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that knows the substance of an expert's anticipated testimony (e.g., from an expert report) must timely object to the expert's qualifications or risk forfeiting the objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opposing party admitted the expert and did not object when the expert was designated/admitted, later objections to qualifications may be forfeited. Example from case: Opti-Luxx did not object to York's admission when Smartrend moved to recognize him as an expert and thus forfeited a later qualifications objection. Practical tip: object to qualifications before the court rules on admission if the report reveals the intended scope of testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for admitting expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's admission of an expert witness is reviewed for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts will not disturb admissibility unless the district court clearly abused its discretion (see Sundance). Practitioners should preserve objections and focus on demonstrating either relevance or lack thereof under Daubert/other admissibility standards as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent claim scope: 'as shown' vs. 'as shown and described'
rubrics_metrics.description: A patented design may be claimed 'as shown' or 'as shown and described.' Where claimed 'as shown and described,' the patent’s scope of protection is limited by both the drawings and the accompanying description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP notes that 'the illustration in the drawing views is its own best description' but allows use of written description to identify appearance for portions not illustrated (MPEP §1503.01(II) and §1503.01(II)(A)(1)). When the specification explicitly describes a feature (e.g., stating oblique shading 'denote[s] transparency'), the description can narrow what otherwise ambiguous drawing conventions might indicate. Anti-pattern: relying solely on drawings where the specification expressly clarifies or limits meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of oblique shading in design drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblique shading in patent drawings may show 'transparent, translucent and highly polished or reflective surfaces' according to MPEP §1503.02(II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But where the specification expressly uses oblique shading to denote a specific feature (e.g., 'transparency'), the written description can narrow the shading's import. Practitioners should not assume oblique shading always equates to a single optical property without checking the specification and relevant MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: plain and ordinary meaning vs. art-specific meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim term is not disclaimed or specially defined in the specification, the jury must apply the plain and ordinary meaning of the term. If a party asserts an art-specific plain and ordinary meaning, it must be established with reliable extrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence may be considered to establish an art-specific meaning but testimony at odds with the written patent record should be afforded no weight (Phillips). Conclusory expert testimony unsupported by objective sources (industry publications, dictionaries) is insufficient (Network Com., Wireless Agents). On remand, district court may determine whether an art-specific meaning exists, but the proponent must produce reliable extrinsic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on extrinsic evidence in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (including expert testimony) that conflicts with the patent's written record should be disregarded in claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must start with intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence can inform meaning only when consistent with intrinsic evidence and supported by reliable sources. Anti-pattern: relying on expert assertions that contradict express statements in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review standard for claim construction and factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction based on intrinsic evidence is reviewed de novo; underlying factual findings based on extrinsic evidence are reviewed for clear error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Phillips and subsequent Federal Circuit precedent: interpret claim terms according to their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSA in the context of the entire patent. Where the district court resolves subsidiary facts from extrinsic evidence, appellate review accords clear-error deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents protect ornamental/aesthetic features and have narrow scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect the ornamental or aesthetic features of a design (35 U.S.C. §171(a)) and are given narrow scope compared to utility patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import functional interpretations into design-patent scope. When construing design claims, focus on drawings and accompanying description; be mindful that courts construe design patents narrowly (Top Brand; Carman Indus.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of structural claim terms using intrinsic evidence (example: 'frame')
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms that are repeatedly and consistently described in the specification (e.g., a 'frame') may be construed narrowly to require a specific structural characteristic (e.g., a 'separate and distinct component').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification 'repeatedly, consistently, and exclusively' refers to a component as separate (see In re Abbott Diabetes Care; Irdeto), the claims should be read to require that separation. Look to the specification's described functions (e.g., 'configured to removably receive the sign') and embodiments (frameless, replaceable lens) to inform construction. Anti-pattern: reading a broad literal scope when the specification consistently points to a narrower structural requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining function for doctrine-of-equivalents analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of a claimed element for DOE can be established by the patent's disclosure; if the patent is silent, courts turn to the ordinarily skilled artisan to determine function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification explicitly teaches certain functions (e.g., removably receiving the sign so it can be serviced or customized), that intrinsic evidence can be dispositive in deciding whether the accused product performs the same function. If the accused device does not perform the patent-disclosed function, DOE infringement fails (Hill-Rom example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents test: insubstantial differences / function-way-result
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE prevents avoiding infringement by changing only minor or insubstantial details. The function-way-result test asks whether the accused product 'performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties may agree on the function-way-result articulation. For DOE to succeed, equivalence must be demonstrated as to each claimed element (Lockheed Martin) and supported by particularized testimony and a linking argument (VLSI Tech.). Anti-pattern: asserting equivalence based on general similarities without element-by-element particularized proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of particularized testimony and linking argument for DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must provide particularized testimony and linking argument showing how each claimed element is equivalent to the accused product's corresponding feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General or conclusory expert testimony that fails to tie the accused structure to the claimed element's disclosed function/way/result is insufficient. Courts require detailed, element-specific analysis (VLSI Tech.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard and review for JMOL in patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: JMOL is appropriate if no reasonable, properly instructed jury could have found for the non-moving party on the issue; appellate review of the denial of JMOL is de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reviewing JMOL, the court must take the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving (prevailing at trial) party (Sundance). If undisputed evidence (including concession by patentee's expert) shows an element's function is not performed by the accused device, no reasonable jury could find equivalence and JMOL should be granted. Practical tip: develop record evidence that either establishes or refutes the claimed function; concessions by experts are dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony cannot contradict the patent's written record; conclusory testimony insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony that is 'at odds with . . . the written record of the patent' should be afforded no weight, and conclusory testimony unsupported by reliable extrinsic material is insufficient for claim construction or equivalence findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should support opinions with objective contemporaneous sources (industry publications, dictionaries, technical references). Absent reliable support, courts may disregard expert statements (Phillips; Network Com.; Wireless Agents). Anti-pattern: relying solely on an expert's ipse dixit to override clear intrinsic disclosure.
